# Agents Guide — TaskForge Vault
<!-- taskforge:generated-by app=TaskForge version=3.0.0 schema=1 -->
<!-- taskforge:generated-at 2026-10-15T01:26:28Z -->
<!-- taskforge:regenerate-on-settings-change true -->

Generated by TaskForge from this vault's Settings. Rewritten automatically
whenever a format-affecting setting changes (inline dialect, field renames,
TaskNotes config, status symbols, archive paths, time format). Do not
hand-edit — your changes are overwritten on the next regenerate.
Disable: **Settings > AI & Agents > Generate agent files > Off** (files are
then removed). Same facts, machine-readable: `dialect.json`.
Spaces (saved filters + creation defaults): `spaces.json`. Resolve these filenames relative to this `agents.md` file, in the configured settings folder.

## Agent quickstart

Prefer the `taskforge` CLI / MCP over raw file edits: it runs THIS vault's real
parser and honors recurrence + archive semantics a hand edit gets wrong. Work
this file-free loop:

1. **Find / dedupe** — `query '<expr>'` (or `id:<ref>`) BEFORE creating, so you
don't duplicate an existing task.
2. **Create** — `add "<title>" [--due …] [--priority …] [--assign-id]`.
`--assign-id` mints a durable stable id you can reference later.
3. **Enrich** — `edit <id> --set-prop k=v --append-note "…" --add-tag …`;
custom props are TYPED on write.
4. **Complete** — `done <id>` (advances recurrence, runs onCompletion — a raw
`[x]` flip would lose the next occurrence).

**Idempotent retry:** `add --upsert --id <ref>` is create-or-update keyed on
`<ref>` — safe to re-run after a timeout without duplicating (`--upsert`
requires `--id`; it rejects `--assign-id`). Read this vault's dialect once with
`dialect --json` (resolved view) or `dialect --raw` (writeback-valid input form).

```taskforge-example-cli
taskforge query 'status:!done due:<next7d' --json
taskforge add "Buy milk" --due 2026-07-10 --assign-id --json
taskforge add --upsert --id weekly-report "Weekly report" --json
taskforge edit <id> --set-prop effort=3 --append-note "context" --json
taskforge done <id> --json
```

### Two ids per task

Every result carries `id` and `stable_id`. `id` is the CORPUS id — path-derived,
and it RE-MINTS on a title/path/created edit (move and convert change it): fine
within one session, don't persist it. `stable_id` is the DURABLE user id
(`🆔`/`id::`) — it survives move/convert, so use it for long-lived references. Any
id-targeting command accepts EITHER, and resolves a unique PREFIX of either (an
ambiguous prefix → exit 2). Mint one with `add --assign-id` (or set your own with
`--id <ref>`); a bare `add` leaves `stable_id` null. `edit`/`update_task` (and
`bulk_update_tasks`) also accept `--assign-id`/`assign_id` (mint-if-missing) or
`--set-id`/`set_id` (an exact ref; errors on a vault-wide collision) on the SAME
call as the rest of your edit.

Every result also carries `deeplink` — a `taskforge:///task/<ref>` URL that opens
the task directly in the TaskForge app. Hand it to the user as a tappable link
when referring them to a specific task.

`status` is the CANONICAL status (`planned`, …), what `status:` and `set_status` take;
`status_label` is what the USER sees, this vault's name for it (`planned` may show as
"In Review"). Quote `status_label` to the user; both spellings are accepted back.

`parent_id`/`depth` (the resolved parent's stable id and nesting depth) are present
on every read (`query_tasks`/`get_task`) AND on every hierarchy-writing call
(`update_task` set_parent/clear_parent, `outdent_task`, `bulk_reparent_tasks`,
`add_task` with `parent`) — `depth: 0`/no `parent_id` key means a resolved ROOT, never
unresolved. BOTH keys are ABSENT from any other response (add without `parent`,
complete_task, etc.): that absence means the command never checked hierarchy, never
a claim the task is a root — call get_task/query_tasks to find out.

**This vault does NOT stamp ids automatically** (`stamp_task_ids` is off) — most tasks have no `stable_id` until one is minted explicitly. A result missing one or more `stable_id`s carries a `warnings` entry saying so; that is expected, not an error. To get one per task without minting by hand, ask the user to enable "Task IDs" in TaskForge settings, or run `taskforge ids stamp` yourself (a CLI-only, explicit, user-consented vault-wide sweep — there is no MCP tool for it by design).

### Response envelope

**CLI** — one JSON object on stdout plus a process exit code: a single task as
`{ok:true, task}`, a list as `{ok:true, tasks, count, next_offset?}`, an error as
`{ok:false, code, message, hint?}`. Branch on the exit code or the stable machine
`code` (`not-found`, `if-hash-mismatch`, `vault-not-found`), never the human `message`.
**MCP** — the SAME data with NO `ok` field: `get_task` → `{task}`, a single mutator →
`{task, …}`, `query_tasks` → `{count, truncated, next_offset?, tasks, partial}`. An
error is the tool result's `is_error:true` flag with a `{code, message, hint}` body
(same `code` vocabulary) — no `ok:false` to test, branch on `is_error`. **List honesty:**
`truncated:true` = matches exceeded `limit` (page with `offset`/`next_offset`);
`partial:true` = a space-scoped query couldn't evaluate every condition exactly.

Task objects carry TYPED `props` (a numeric custom prop reads back a JSON number, a
list an array), plus `body`, `created`, `completed` — so you never open the file to
read them. `query`/`ls` omit `body` by default; pass `--include-body` (MCP
`include_body`). **Pagination:** `--offset N` skips N of the sorted set (with
`--limit`); `count` is the full pre-limit total, `next_offset` the next page's offset
(omitted once exhausted).

## Tools & verbs

Every operation is one MCP tool and its identical CLI verb — same engine, same on-disk result. The full catalog (generated from the live tool router, so it can't go stale):

| Tool | Group | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `add_task` | create | create one task (typed props, placement, recurrence); parent resolves parent_id/depth |
| `bulk_add_tasks` | create | create many in one call (best-effort per item) |
| `query_tasks` | read | search/filter with the query grammar; sorted + paginated |
| `get_task` | read | fetch one task by id (+ content_hash for if_hash edits) |
| `get_tasks` | read | fetch many tasks by id in one call (best-effort per id) |
| `update_task` | edit | edit fields, set/clear props, set/clear parent (returns resolved parent_id/depth) |
| `bulk_update_tasks` | edit | apply one field patch to many |
| `complete_task` | lifecycle | mark done; advances recurrence, runs onCompletion; flags was_dependency_blocked |
| `bulk_complete_tasks` | lifecycle | complete many; per-item was_dependency_blocked flag |
| `archive_task` | lifecycle | move a task to the archive target |
| `delete_task` | lifecycle | delete one (needs confirm_title — hallucinated-id guard) |
| `bulk_delete_tasks` | lifecycle | delete many (needs acknowledge:true; dry-run first) |
| `move_task` | structure | move a task to another file/section |
| `bulk_move_tasks` | structure | move many |
| `move_note` | structure | rename/move any markdown file by path (plain note or TaskNotes) |
| `delete_note` | structure | delete a note by path → .trash/ + unlink refs (needs confirm_title) |
| `create_note` | structure | create a note; --daily appends to today's daily note |
| `read_note` | read | read a note's body as addressable blocks + whole-file digest |
| `patch_note_block` | edit | edit one note block by stable_id, conflict-checked |
| `update_note` | edit | replace a note's whole content, digest-guarded |
| `patch_note_frontmatter` | edit | set/remove one frontmatter key, digest-guarded |
| `convert_task` | structure | convert inline line ↔ TaskNotes file |
| `bulk_convert_tasks` | structure | convert many |
| `outdent_task` | structure | promote a task one level; returns the resolved parent_id/depth |
| `bulk_reparent_tasks` | structure | reparent/promote many; each outcome carries the resolved parent_id/depth |
| `lint_task` | utility | validate candidate lines against this vault's dialect |
| `normalize_references` | utility | convert every link-valued parent / blockedBy reference to a task id, and put every parent in one encoding |
| `doctor` | utility | report vault health (dialect/spaces presence, writability) |
| `list_spaces` | utility | enumerate saved spaces (+ optional membership counts) |
| `get_dialect` | utility | read this vault's write dialect + valid status/priority values |

Prefer the MCP tools when your agent has an MCP connection — typed args, structured errors you can self-correct against, no `taskforge` on `PATH`. Use the CLI in shell contexts with no MCP (scripts, cron, CI, a coding agent in a repo). Editing vault files by hand is the last resort — it bypasses recurrence + archive semantics.

### Recurring tasks — completing vs SKIPPING an occurrence

`done`/`complete_task` COMPLETES an occurrence (stamps a completion date, fires
`onCompletion`, advances the series). To record a **skipped** occurrence, use the
EDIT surface instead — `edit <id> --skip-occurrence` (CLI) /
`update_task {skip_occurrence}` (MCP). There is deliberately NO skip flag on
`done`/`complete_task`: a skip is an edit to the series, not a completion, so it
flips no status, writes no completion date, and fires no `onCompletion`.
Pass `YYYY-MM-DD` for a specific instance, or no value for the task's anchor date
(scheduled → due → start). Mutually exclusive with `--set-status` and
`--recurrence`/`--clear-recurrence`. The skipped-instances field is core-written —
never edit it yourself.

### Bulk mutations & guards

Bulk tools/verbs act on many tasks; each takes EXACTLY ONE of `ids` (an explicit
list) or `query`. A `query`-targeted commit is refused unless you pass
`acknowledge_count` (MCP) / `--acknowledge-count N` (CLI) equal to the exact match
count — a blast-radius guard against a broad `query` like `status:!done`. Run
`dry_run:true` / `--dry-run` first: it writes nothing and reports the count, then
repeat with that count. Targeting by `ids` needs no count. `bulk_delete_tasks`
also needs `acknowledge:true` because deletion cannot be undone.

**`acknowledge_ids` — the stronger guard; prefer it.** A count proves
HOW MANY tasks match, not WHICH — a concurrent vault change that swaps one member
keeps the count valid and mutates the wrong task. Pass the EXACT ids from your
preview instead — `acknowledge_ids` on EVERY MCP bulk tool (`bulk_delete_tasks`,
`bulk_move_tasks`, `bulk_convert_tasks`, `bulk_reparent_tasks`,
`bulk_update_tasks`), and `--acknowledge-id A --acknowledge-id B` (or
comma-separated `--acknowledge-id A,B`) on EVERY CLI bulk verb (`rm`, `move`,
`convert`, `reparent`, `edit`): the commit re-resolves the query and refuses
unless the match set is IDENTICAL. It satisfies the acknowledgement requirement
on its own — pass it INSTEAD of `acknowledge_count`, not alongside.

### Streams & exit codes

**Streams (CLI):** stdout carries ONLY the JSON object; human diagnostics and
logs go to stderr. Read stdout alone — never capture `2>&1`, or the human line
corrupts the JSON your parser reads.

**Exit codes (CLI)** — branch on these; a read is `0` even with zero matches:

- `0` success (incl. empty result — a read that matched nothing is still 0) · `2` malformed/ambiguous command — fix + re-issue · `64` usage error (bad args, empty bulk query) · `65` unparseable value/grammar — fix the value · `66` target not found (task id / space) — re-target · `74` filesystem I/O error · `75` retryable `--if-hash` conflict — re-read then retry · `78` vault/config problem (no vault, schema too old, missing spaces, settings unreadable or quarantined — see `taskforge doctor`)

## Query grammar reference

`taskforge query '<expr>'` (CLI) and the `query_tasks` MCP tool take the same
filter grammar — a projection of the app's canonical filter matrix, evaluated
only against TASKS. Whitespace = **AND**; `OR`, `NOT`, and `( )` group. Values
with spaces must be quoted (`text:"buy milk"`). Bare words are rejected. An
unknown token or value is an error (exit 65), never silently ignored.

### Tokens

Every row below is generated from the one canonical token registry, so this
table always matches exactly what the parser accepts. `note-*`/`event-*`
filter fields exist in the app's filter matrix but are NOT usable here — this
grammar only ever evaluates against tasks, so a note/event token is rejected
with a loud error (exit 64) instead of silently matching nothing.

| Token | Values | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status:` | todo, done, cancelled, in_progress, on_hold, planned, deferred, blocked, someday, ready, open, closed | status equals (prefix `!` = not); `open`/`closed` match any non-terminal/terminal status | `status:!done` |
| `priority:` | highest, high, medium (med), low, lowest, none | priority equals; also `!name` and ordinal `>=`/`<=`/`>`/`<` | `priority:>=high` |
| `due:` | date grammar | due-date filter | `due:<next7d` |
| `overdue:` | true, false | task is overdue | `overdue:true` |
| `scheduled:` | date grammar (also `pending`/`!pending`) | scheduled-date filter | `scheduled:pending` |
| `pending:` | true, false | shortcut = scheduled OR start pending | `pending:true` |
| `start:` | date grammar (also `pending`/`!pending`) | start-date filter | `start:none` |
| `created:` | date grammar | created-date filter | `created:<prev30d` |
| `completed:` | date grammar | completion-date filter (unions TaskNotes complete instances) | `completed:none` |
| `modified:` | date grammar | modified-date filter | `modified:>2026-01-01` |
| `cancelled:` | date grammar | cancelled-date filter | `cancelled:before-today` |
| `happens:` | date grammar | happens-date filter (earliest of start/scheduled/due) | `happens:today` |
| `duetime:` | <HH:MM (before) / >HH:MM (after) | due time-of-day before/after | `duetime:<09:30` |
| `scheduledtime:` | <HH:MM (before) / >HH:MM (after) | scheduled time-of-day before/after | `scheduledtime:>12:00` |
| `starttime:` | <HH:MM (before) / >HH:MM (after) | start time-of-day before/after | `starttime:<08:00` |
| `tag:` | text (prefix `!` not, `~` substring, `=` only-this); `none`/`any` = has none / has any | accent-folded tag match | `tag:work` |
| `context:` | text (prefix `!` not, `~` substring, `=` only-this); `none`/`any` = has none / has any | accent-folded context match | `context:office` |
| `project:` | text (prefix `!` not, `~` substring, `=` only-this); `none`/`any` = has none / has any | accent-folded project match | `project:~launch` |
| `text:` | quoted text (prefix `=` exact, `^` starts, `$` ends, `!` not — title) | title OR description contains | `text:"buy milk"` |
| `desc:` | quoted text (prefix `!` = not) | description contains | `desc:"quarterly report"` |
| `file:` | text (prefix `=` exact, `~` substring, `!` not) | note file name (basename) | `file:groceries` |
| `path:` | text (prefix `=` exact, `^` starts, `$` ends, `~` substring, `!` not) | vault-relative file path contains | `path:^Projects/` |
| `recurring:` | true, false | task has any recurrence rule | `recurring:true` |
| `recurs:` | daily, weekly, monthly, yearly | recurrence unit equals | `recurs:weekly` |
| `recurrence-interval:` | positive integer | recurrence interval equals (e.g. every 2 weeks) | `recurrence-interval:2` |
| `recurrence-basis:` | due, scheduled, start | recurrence base date equals | `recurrence-basis:due` |
| `recurrence-weekday:` | true, false | recurrence is weekday-based | `recurrence-weekday:true` |
| `recurrence-based-on-completion:` | true, false | recurrence advances from completion date | `recurrence-based-on-completion:true` |
| `subtask:` | true, false | task is a subtask (false = top-level) | `subtask:true` |
| `has-subtasks:` | true, false | task has child subtasks | `has-subtasks:true` |
| `parent-complete:` | true, false | parent task is complete | `parent-complete:false` |
| `parent-open:` | true, false | parent task is open (not complete) | `parent-open:true` |
| `all-subtasks-complete:` | true, false | every child subtask is complete | `all-subtasks-complete:true` |
| `any-subtask-open:` | true, false | at least one child subtask is still open | `any-subtask-open:true` |
| `blocking:` | true, false | task blocks another (open dependents) | `blocking:true` |
| `has-dependents:` | true, false | task has any dependents | `has-dependents:true` |
| `blocked:` | true, false | task is blocked: status blocked, or a dependency on an open task (one naming no task does not count) | `blocked:true` |
| `has-deps:` | true, false | task has dependencies | `has-deps:true` |
| `daily-note:` | true, false, today, !today | task lives in a daily note (`today` = today's note) | `daily-note:today` |
| `oncompletion:` | keep, delete, archive (prefix `!` = not) | on-completion action equals | `oncompletion:archive` |
| `source:` | inline, tasknotes (prefix `!` = not) | storage type equals (inline markdown vs TaskNotes) | `source:tasknotes` |
| `prop:` | key | key=v | key!=v | key~v | key>=n | key>n | key<n | key<=n | key>DATE | key<DATE (=/!=/~ string; ~ on a list = element-equals; >=/>/</<= numeric; >/< DATE; =true boolean) | custom property existence / value | `prop:report_count>=3` |
| `id:` | stable id or corpus id (prefix `!` = not) | resolve a task by its stable id OR corpus id | `id:mra08yqv` |
| `stable_id:` | the `stable_id` value this surface's own `query`/`get_task` output emits (prefix `!` = not) | alias of `id:` — resolve a task by its stable id OR corpus id | `stable_id:mra08yqv` |

Status names: todo, done, cancelled, in_progress, on_hold, planned, deferred, blocked, someday, ready. Priority names: highest, high, medium (med), low, lowest, none.

**Date value grammar** (every date field accepts all of these):
`today` · `tomorrow` · `+Nd` · `YYYY-MM-DD` (equals) · `<YYYY-MM-DD` (before) · `>YYYY-MM-DD` (after) ·
`before-today` · `after-today` · `none` (no date) · `any` (has a date) ·
`<nextNd` (within the next N days) · `<prevNd` (within the previous N days).
`pending`/`!pending` is accepted on `scheduled:`/`start:` only; prefix `!` to negate ANY value above (`!today`, `!tomorrow`, `!+7d`, ...) instead of a dedicated `not_today` op.

**Time value grammar** (`duetime:`/`scheduledtime:`/`starttime:`): `<HH:MM`
(before that wall-clock time) or `>HH:MM` (after). There is no equals form.

**Feeding output back in.** Result `file_path` is a full vault-relative path,
so it pairs with `path:` — NOT `file:`, which matches the basename only (a
value containing `/` is rejected, exit 65, not silently unmatched). Every
other field round-trips through its same-named token; `tags`/`contexts`/
`projects` come back bare, with no `#`/`@`/`+` sigil or wikilink brackets.

### Sort

Results sort by one of: due, priority, created (default `due`).

## Vault file format (raw-edit fallback)

Everything below is this vault's on-disk format — you need it only when neither
the CLI nor MCP is available and you must edit files by hand.

## Inline task lines — Obsidian Tasks emoji format

This vault writes Obsidian-Tasks emoji tokens, not `[key:: value]` fields.

```taskforge-example
- [ ] Buy groceries
- [ ] Ship v2 release 📅 2026-07-15 ⏫
- [ ] Water the plants 🔁 every week
- [ ] Draft proposal #writing @desk +[[Q3 Roadmap]]
- [ ] Plan launch
  - [ ] Write announcement #writing
  - [x] Book venue
```

## Emoji token table

| token | meaning |
|---|---|
| 📅 | due date |
| ⏳ | scheduled date |
| 🛫 | start date |
| ✅ | done date |
| ❌ | cancelled date |
| ➕ | created date |
| 🔺 / ⏫ / 🔼 / 🔽 / ⏬ | priority (highest→lowest) |
| 🔁 | recurrence (natural language, e.g. `every week`) |
| 🔢 | recurrence limit |
| 🆔 | task id |
| ⛔ | depends on |

Status checkboxes: `[ ]` todo · `[x]` done · `[-]` cancelled · `[/]` in progress · `[!]` on hold · `[>]` planned · `[~]` deferred · `[#]` blocked · `[?]` someday · `[*]` ready. Time format: **12-hour**. Tags `#a/b`
(hierarchical), contexts `@ctx`, projects `+name` or `+[[Wikilink]]`.

**Both notations are read regardless of format:** a Dataview bracket
(`[due:: 2026-09-23]`) is typed metadata here just as the emoji token is — but
this vault WRITES emoji, so prefer the tokens above; an edit re-serializes each
field as emoji, keeping an untouched bracket token in its own notation.

## TaskNotes task-files (frontmatter)

One file = one task, lives under **`TaskNotes/Tasks`**. Identified by the `#task` tag (in the file's `tags:` frontmatter or body).
Status values: `open|done|cancelled|in-progress|on-hold|planned|deferred|blocked|someday|ready`. Priority values: `highest|high|normal|low|lowest|none`.
Full field list: `dialect.json`.

## Archive

Completed inline tasks move to `TaskForge-Archive.md`. Completed TaskNotes
files move to the `TaskNotes/Archive/` folder.
A space with its own storage settings can name its own archive file and folder;
its tasks archive there (`--space`/MCP `space` picks one).

## Additional properties

A property beyond the field tables above can still be recorded and is
preserved verbatim (see Rules). Inline: [key:: value] or (key:: value) on the task line. TaskNotes:
any unrecognized YAML key on a TaskNotes file round-trips verbatim. Accepted inline key shape: `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*` —
letter-first, then letters/digits/underscores (e.g. `priority_label`).
Values are TYPED on write (numbers/bools stay unquoted; `sku="3"`
forces a string). Repeated same-key `--prop`/`--set-prop` (or a CSV
value) ACCUMULATE into a list — parity with `--tag`: `k=a k=b` and
`k=a,b` both yield `[a, b]`, a lone scalar stays scalar, elements keep
their type. MCP `props`/`set_props` is a JSON object (no repeat keys) —
use the CSV form there.

Converting a TaskNotes file to inline preserves unknown frontmatter keys
as `[key:: value]` (casing verbatim) when the value is a single-line
scalar; a structured or multi-line value has no inline form and is
refused before either file changes. A CLI dry run lists proposed losses
in `dropped_fields`; it does not authorize a lossy write.

## Where new tasks go

New inline tasks are appended to `TaskForge.md`.

New TaskNotes files are created in `TaskNotes/Tasks`; the filename is
the task title, sanitized (format: `title`).

New tasks must include this vault's required tags: `#task`.

## Notes

New notes are created at the vault ROOT (no notes folder is configured). Daily notes are named by this vault's date format `YYYY-MM-DD` — e.g. today's note is `2026-07-20.md`. `create_note --daily` (MCP `create_note` with `daily:true`) resolves TODAY'S note by that format and appends `--content` to it — creating it (from the configured template, if any) when absent. Prefer it over hand-computing the filename.

### Note verbs

- **Create** — `add-note "<title>"` (MCP `create_note`) writes a new file; `--daily` appends to today's daily note instead.
- **Rename / move** — `mv-note <path> <dest>` (MCP `move_note`) is THE safe way to rename or move a note: it rewrites every `dependsOn`/`projects` and body `[[wikilink]]`/`[display](path)` reference to follow the file. **Never** `mv`/rename the file raw — that dangles every reference to it.
- **Delete** — `rm-note <path> --yes` (MCP `delete_note`) is THE safe way to delete a note: it moves the file to `.trash/` and strips/unlinks every reference vault-wide. **Never** `rm` the file raw.
- **Read the body** — `read-note <path>` (MCP `read_note`) returns the note's blocks with stable ids + the whole-file digest.
- **Edit the body** — `patch-note` (MCP `patch_note_block`) for one block, `update-note` (MCP `update_note`) for the whole file. See below.

### Editing a note's body

`read-note <path>` returns each block with a `stable_id`, `kind`, `index`, `depth`, `parent_id` and verbatim `raw`, plus the file's `content_digest`. Target a block by its `stable_id`; the ids are content-derived, so they change when a block's text changes — always re-read before a new edit.

**Always get → digest → write.** Both write verbs REQUIRE `--expected-digest` (MCP `expected_digest`) — the `content_digest` from the `read-note` you based the edit on. This is not optional the way task `--if-hash` is: it is how a concurrent edit is detected instead of silently clobbered.

| op | payload | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `replace` | `new_raw`: string (markdown) | replace a block's text (prose, heading, list item) (refused on task lines) |
| `insert` | `new_raw`: string (markdown), `position?`: before | after | child_of | insert a new block before/after/under the target |
| `delete` | — | delete the target block (refused on task lines) |
| `split` | `offset`: integer (character offset) | split the target block in two at a character offset (refused on task lines) |
| `merge` | `second_id`: string (block id) | merge the target block with the one after it |
| `indent` | — | indent a list/task item one level |
| `outdent` | — | outdent a list/task item one level |

**Conflicts.** `patch-note` classifies every write against your digest, four ways:

- `clean` — the file is byte-identical to what you read; the edit applies.
- `disk_changed_elsewhere` — the file moved, but YOUR block is untouched. Refused by default; pass `--on-conflict allow_untouched_block` to apply it anyway.
- `block_changed` — your block also changed on disk. Never applied; the error carries `disk_raw` (the disk's current text) so you can rebase and retry.
- `block_gone` — your block no longer exists, or can't be identified with confidence. Never applied; re-read and re-target.

Echo `base_block` (`--base-index`/`--base-count`/`--base-kind`/`--base-raw`) from the `read-note` response to get the full classification on a file that changed; omit it and an unresolvable target is reported as `block_gone` rather than risking a wrong-block write.

**Task lines are off limits here.** `patch-note --op replace`, `--op delete` and `--op split` are REFUSED on a `task`-kind block — editing a task's text, removing it, or slicing its raw line in two through the note surface would bypass dialect serialization and lint. Use `update` (MCP `update_task`) to change a task's text or fields, `done` (`complete_task`) for its status, and `rm` (`delete_task`) to remove it. `insert`, `merge`, `indent` and `outdent` stay available — they restructure a list without rewriting a task line.

**`--op delete` removes ONE block, not a subtree.** Deleting a list item or heading leaves its children in place; they become effective roots and re-flow on the next reparse. There is no delete-subtree op — walk the children from `read-note` and delete them yourself (deepest first) if that is what you meant.

**`update_note` will not rename a task.** On a TaskNotes file it refuses to change the frontmatter title, because a title change re-mints the task's id — route it through `update_task`. Frontmatter is outside `patch-note`'s jurisdiction entirely.

Notes above 5 MiB are refused by all three verbs. `--dry-run` previews a patch or update without writing.

### Rules of engagement

- **Editing a note's BODY directly in the file is safe** — TaskForge's parser is lossless, so prose/heading/list edits round-trip untouched. A `[[wikilink]]` target resolves SHORTEST-PATH first: a bare basename matches the shortest unique path (Obsidian-style).
- Use `mv-note` for renames and `rm-note` for deletes (above) — a raw `mv`/`rm` leaves dangling references the parser can't repair.
- `settings.json` and `spaces.json` are **app-owned** — never hand-edit them; change these through the TaskForge app.
- After a bulk note change, run `doctor` (MCP `doctor`) to surface any dangling references left behind.
- **Spaces are app-only** (D-SPACES): there is no agent verb to create/rename/delete a space or its sections; don't edit `spaces.json`. Query a space with `ls --space <id>`.
- **Calendar events are out of reach** (D-EVENTS): device-calendar events are not vault files, so no CLI/MCP verb can read or write them — that is permanent, not a gap.
## Spaces

Spaces are saved filters + creation defaults, defined in
`spaces.json`. Follow each space's `add_recipe` to add a task.

## Rules for agents

- **Preserve unknown fields.** Any token or YAML key you don't recognize
round-trips verbatim — don't strip it.
- Prefer atomic writes (temp file + rename) for files in this vault.

content:
<!-- taskforge-generator: app 3.0.2 -->
# TaskForge vault settings

TaskForge keeps your settings as plain JSON in this folder — `TaskForge/Settings/`, nested one level inside `TaskForge/` at the root of your vault — so they travel with your notes and can be read or edited by hand, by another tool, or by an AI agent. Nothing here is a database or a cache you must not touch: `settings.json` and the files under `spaces/` are yours to edit. The `TaskForge/` folder itself is otherwise entirely yours — put your own notes there.

Older versions of TaskForge put these files directly in `TaskForge/` (or, further back, in a hidden `.taskforge/` folder). Either is migrated into this nested `Settings/` folder automatically; you should not have more than one copy.

## What is in this folder

| File | What it is | Edit by hand? |
|---|---|---|
| `settings.json` | The one shared settings file, grouped into sections. | Yes |
| `settings.schema.json` | Generated JSON Schema for the above, plus a `defaults` block listing every setting's built-in default. | No — regenerated |
| `README.md` | This file. | No — regenerated |
| `spaces/<slug>.json` | One file per space (your saved lists, boards and filters). | Yes |
| `space-deletions.json` | Timestamped records saying a space was deleted. See "Deleting a space". | Yes, carefully |
| `devices/<clientId>.json` | Settings belonging to one physical install. | Rarely |
| `agents.md`, `dialect.json`, `spaces.json` | Generated contract files describing this vault to the TaskForge CLI, the MCP server and AI agents. `spaces.json` is the one they read to know what your spaces are. | No — regenerated by the app; see below before deleting them |
| `settings.broken-*.json`, `settings.conflict-*.json`, `settings.replaced-*.json` | Preserved copies of earlier settings. See "When something goes wrong". | No |

**The three generated contract files are regenerated by the app, not by the CLI.** Deleting `spaces.json` therefore does not just cost you a file that comes straight back: `taskforge spaces`, every `--space` option and the MCP `list_spaces` tool have nothing to read, and the whole spaces surface stays unavailable until the vault is next opened in the TaskForge app. The same is true of `dialect.json`, which is how those tools learn your status symbols and field names.

## Editing these files

- **Edits are picked up automatically**, usually within about a second: TaskForge watches this folder while it is running. A periodic re-check every 60 seconds is kept as a backstop, so an edit is never lost even where the watcher cannot see it — on iOS there is no folder watcher at all and that periodic check is the only mechanism, so allow up to a minute there.
- **You do not need to touch `updatedAt`.** Changes to `settings.json` are detected from the file's *content*. The app maintains `updatedAt` for its own conflict resolution; editing it by hand neither helps nor hurts.
- **Unknown keys are preserved.** A key this version of the app does not recognise is left exactly as written, never dropped — so a newer release's settings survive being opened by an older one, and third-party tooling can annotate the file safely. The same is true of an unrecognised *value*: a status name or format this build does not understand is kept verbatim rather than being reset to the default.
- **One deliberate exception:** a key TaskForge *removed* in an earlier version is not resurrected. Preserving keys is about the future, not about undoing a deletion.
- **To reset a setting, write its default value; deleting a key does not reset it.** A key missing from the file keeps the value each device already has, and TaskForge writes it back.
- **Write valid JSON.** If the file cannot be parsed, TaskForge will not silently repair or replace it — see below.
- See `settings.schema.json` in this folder for the exact type and accepted values of every key.

## Which settings live where

Every setting belongs to exactly one of seven classes. The class decides which file holds it and whether it follows you, the vault, or the machine:

| Class | Follows | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| **bootstrap** | the install | local storage — it is what *finds* the vault, so it has to be readable before any file in the vault can be. Its value is also mirrored into this install's own `devices/<clientId>.json`, where you will see it listed; that copy travels with the vault but is never what locates it |
| **user-global** | you | `settings.json`, and roams to your other devices via iCloud |
| **vault-dialect** | this vault | `settings.json` — **never roams** |
| **vault-path** | this vault | `settings.json` — **never roams** |
| **vault-workflow** | this vault | `settings.json` — **never roams** |
| **device-local** | this machine | `devices/<clientId>.json` |
| **device-vault** | this machine, for this vault | `devices/<clientId>.json` |

**The dialect settings are the important ones.** "Dialect" means everything that decides the actual bytes written into your notes: your status symbols, whether tasks are inline or TaskNotes-style, your TaskNotes frontmatter field names, the daily-note filename format, and the rules for reading a date out of a filename. Those are a property of **this vault**, not of you. They stay in this file, they are included in backups, and they are deliberately NOT synced to your other devices through iCloud — so opening a second vault with different conventions can no longer overwrite them. Two devices open on the *same* vault still converge, through this file.

Not everything about appearance is scoped to this vault. Your custom status names, your priority names and your priority colours are display-only — they change no bytes in your notes — so they stay user-global and roam with you. The status symbols those names label do **not** roam, because they are written into your files. Both sit in `settings.json`, in their own sections.

Switching to a different vault asks whether to carry your setup over. Nothing is copied silently.

## Versions: `schemaVersion` and `compatVersion`

`settings.json` carries two numbers. `schemaVersion` records the structure the file was written with. `compatVersion` is a floor: the oldest app version that can still write this file back without losing anything.
An app older than the `compatVersion` floor treats the file as **read-only**. It still reads and applies every setting, but it will not write to the file — so a change made on that device applies locally and can never reach your other devices. TaskForge says so in the app rather than letting the two drift apart quietly. Updating that device is the fix.
A file with no `schemaVersion` at all — hand-written, or from before versioning existed — is read for the keys it actually contains. TaskForge will not fill in the rest from its built-in defaults, because "absent" is not the same as "set to the default".

## When something goes wrong

**A file that cannot be parsed is never overwritten.** If `settings.json` stops being valid JSON, TaskForge stops writing settings entirely, keeps a copy as `settings.broken-<timestamp>.json`, and shows a banner offering to open the file or to replace it with the settings the app currently holds. It waits and re-reads first: a file that is still downloading from iCloud looks broken for a moment, so nothing is reported until the contents have stopped changing.
Choosing **Replace** preserves what was there as `settings.replaced-<timestamp>.json` before writing anything new. If that copy cannot be made, the replace is refused rather than done.
**Sync conflict copies** — the extra files Dropbox, iCloud, Obsidian Sync or Syncthing leave behind when two devices write at once — are detected and resolved automatically. The newest wins, judged by the `updatedAt` recorded *inside* each file rather than by the filesystem's timestamp, which sync engines rewrite. The losing copy is kept as `settings.conflict-<timestamp>.json`.
None of these copies are ever deleted while they might matter: a sidecar is removed only once it is more than 90 days old, and the three most recent of each kind are kept regardless of age.

**While settings are quarantined, TaskForge refuses to write markdown rather than guess.** It cannot know your status symbols or field names, and writing the wrong ones into your notes is worse than doing nothing:

- The generated `dialect.json` is rewritten to a stub carrying `"quarantined"` and `"dialect_version": 0`. The TaskForge CLI and the MCP server both stop writing to the vault while that marker is present — including older builds that predate the marker, which stop on the version instead. Because the stub leaves them nothing to read your task formats with, they stop reading too rather than answer from built-in defaults. Fix the settings file in the app and the marker clears.
- The marker is a shortcut, not the mechanism. The CLI and the MCP server read this `settings.json` themselves, so they reach the same conclusion from the same file with no marker involved: they stop when it is present, non-empty, and still fails to parse a moment later. That covers the cases a marker cannot — when you have turned off generating these agent files (there is no `dialect.json` to mark), when this folder has been renamed — they find it by looking for the `settings.json`, and if two folders here hold one they stop rather than pick — and when the file was edited while the app was closed, so nothing was running to mark anything. They resume the moment the file parses again.
- How much they stop depends on whether `dialect.json` is still there. If it is, it is what actually describes your formats, so reading keeps working normally and every answer carries a warning that the description may be out of date; only writing stops. If there is no usable `dialect.json`, reading stops as well, because the alternative is answering from built-in defaults that may not be your formats — a wrong answer that looks exactly like a right one.
- `taskforge doctor` always runs, on every one of these states. It is what you run because something is broken, so it never refuses: it names the file, quotes the error, and states both ways out.
- **Mid-write and empty are not the same as broken**, and they do not get the same message. Only bytes that read cleanly and still fail to parse are called broken. A file that is being written, or empty, or that cannot be read at all, is re-read a few times first — about a second across three attempts, against roughly three seconds in the app, because a command has to answer where the app can wait and try again later. If nothing can be established by the end of that, they still stop rather than guess, but they say which it was: "still being written", "was empty every time it was read", or the permission error itself. Unlike the app, they never recreate an empty settings file — they have no settings of their own to write.
- Ticking a checkbox in a home-screen or Today widget refuses too. The checkbox snaps back and you get a notification or toast saying why — it does not silently do nothing, and it does not write a guess. Widgets keep *displaying* your tasks throughout.

## Spaces

Each space is one file in `spaces/`, named after its slug but identified by the `id` inside it. Editing one is picked up like any other change here. A space file that fails to parse is kept and reported, never rewritten and never deleted — so a typo costs you nothing but a fix.

**Deleting a space** is the one thing you cannot express by deleting its file. A missing file is indistinguishable from one that has not finished syncing, and honouring that would let a half-synced folder erase your spaces with no way back. Instead, deletions are recorded in `space-deletions.json` with the time they happened, and a record only outranks a space that is older than it. Deleting a space in the app writes that record for you; to do it by hand, add the entry there rather than removing the file.

## Premium settings

Settings belonging to premium features are stored in this file whatever your subscription status, and are never stripped out — let a subscription lapse and resume it, and your configuration is still here. Whether a given value **takes effect** is decided when it is read, by whichever part of TaskForge is reading it, so treat the presence of a value in this file as a record of your preference rather than a guarantee that it is currently active.

## Device files

`devices/<clientId>.json` holds settings belonging to one physical install — window geometry, interface scale, per-install bookkeeping, and the handful of choices that are per-device *and* per-vault, such as which space this device shows in its widgets. These never roam and are not part of a portable backup. Unlike `settings.json`, a hand-edit here is only noticed if you also advance its `updatedAt`.

A file in `devices/` that has not been updated for 180 days is removed automatically, so a retired machine does not leave an orphan behind. The current device's own file is never removed, and a file whose timestamp is missing or unreadable is always kept.

# PROYECTO ORCHESTRATOR - Documento maestro

Ultima actualizacion: 2026-10-12
Estado: FUNCIONAL - 95% completado
Duracion total: ~16 horas distribuidas en 2 sesiones

---

## 1. OBJETIVO

Sistema multi-agente en Telegram basado en perfiles persistentes de Hermes:

- Orchestrator: coordinador principal
- Research: investigacion con busqueda web real + APA 7
- Writer: redaccion profesional con fidelidad de fuentes
- Developer: ingenieria y automatizacion

Cada agente con:
- SOUL.md propio (identidad y reglas)
- MEMORY.md independiente
- Honcho aislado (peerName unico)
- Reglas especificas por rol

---

## 2. ARQUITECTURA FINAL

Gateway multiplex (1 proceso unico, PID compartido)

  default      (bot viejo - SIN tocar desde el dia 1)
    Chat privado: 1259111323

  orchestrator (bot nuevo @HermesPro)
    Chat privado: 1259111323
    Grupo "Hermes GPC" (-1003827830738):
      Tema General    (thread_id 1)  -> orchestrator
      Tema research   (thread_id 11) -> research
      Tema writer     (thread_id 12) -> writer
      Tema developer  (thread_id 13) -> developer

  research     (servido via tema 11, tambien via /p/research/)
  writer       (servido via tema 12, tambien via /p/writer/)
  developer    (servido via tema 13, tambien via /p/developer/)

API Server multiplexado:
  http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1/models       (default)
  http://127.0.0.1:8788/p/research/     (research)
  http://127.0.0.1:8788/p/writer/       (writer)
  http://127.0.0.1:8788/p/developer/    (developer)

Plugin hermes-herald: instalado en orchestrator (12 tools)

---

## 3. RUTAS Y CONFIGURACIONES

### Estructura de archivos

/home/droidmaster/.hermes/
  config.yaml                    (config RAIZ - contiene profile_routes)
  SOUL.md                        (del default, intacto desde 2026-10-01)
  memories/
    MEMORY.md                    (del default, 2221 bytes)
    USER.md                      (del default, 646 bytes)
  honcho.json                    (peerName: GePeCasanova-default)
  PROYECTO-ORCHESTRATOR.md       (este documento)
  kanban.db                      (dispatcher activo)
  gateway_state.json
  profiles/
    orchestrator/
      SOUL.md                    (~8433 bytes, 7 secciones)
      MEMORY.md                  (~2000 bytes)
      USER.md                    (~510 bytes)
      config.yaml                (~700 bytes)
      .env                       (tokens + 4 API keys Herald)
      honcho.json                (peerName: GePeCasanova-orchestrator)
      hermes-herald-runs.json    (ledger de dispatch)
      plugins/hermes-herald/     (plugin instalado)
    research/
      SOUL.md                    (~5643 bytes, reglas APA estrictas)
      .env                       (RESEARCH_KEY)
      honcho.json                (peerName: GePeCasanova-research)
    writer/
      SOUL.md                    (~4502 bytes, fidelidad fuentes)
      .env                       (WRITER_KEY)
      honcho.json                (peerName: GePeCasanova-writer)
    developer/
      SOUL.md                    (~1632 bytes)
      .env                       (DEVELOPER_KEY)
      honcho.json                (peerName: GePeCasanova-developer)

### Config RAIZ - bloques clave

profile_routes (agregado 2026-10-11):
  - topic-research: chat_id -1003827830738, thread_id 11, bot_profile orchestrator
  - topic-writer:   chat_id -1003827830738, thread_id 12, bot_profile orchestrator
  - topic-developer: chat_id -1003827830738, thread_id 13, bot_profile orchestrator

platforms.api_server (agregado 2026-10-12):
  enabled: true
  host: 127.0.0.1
  port: 8788
  key: <SHARED_KEY de 64 hex>

kanban.dispatch_in_gateway: true (habilitado 2026-10-11, pendiente desactivar)

fallback.min_switch_reset_seconds: 120 (agregado 2026-10-12)

---

## 4. SOUL.md DEL ORCHESTRATOR (7 secciones)

### Seccion 1 - Identidad (lineas 1-21)

Tu nombre es Orchestrator. Agente principal y coordinador de equipo.
Datos de GePeCasanova: medico, maestria + especialidad UCIP.
Zona horaria GMT-04:00 Cuba. Horario 8am-4pm.
Equipo: Research (busqueda), Writer (redaccion), Developer (herramientas).

### Seccion 2 - Reglas de cron jobs (lineas 22-49)

- Clasificar jobs como monitoreo o informe
- Monitoreo: agregar [SILENT] al prompt
- Informe: NO silenciar
- Preguntar antes de crear un job
- Al auditar: proponer cambios ANTES de aplicar

### Seccion 3 - Reglas de adjuntos (lineas 50-67)

- Guardar en ANEXOS/ con nombre descriptivo
- NUNCA usar nombres temporales tipo img_hash.jpg
- El enlace en la nota DEBE coincidir con el nombre final
- Verificar que el enlace apunte a archivo real

### Seccion 4 - Reglas SD externa (lineas 68-104)

- SD externa: SOLO LECTURA por politica
- Ruta: /mnt/sdcard/ o /storage/0433-100E/
- Prohibido escribir, modificar, borrar o mover archivos
- Si el usuario pide escribir: avisar y sugerir copiar a ANEXOS/
- Zonas protegidas: ObsidianCD/, 01-IMBOX-SD/, 02-RECURSOS/, 03-ARCHIVO/

### Seccion 5 - Reglas APA 7 (lineas 105-127)

- Citas en texto: (Apellido, año), (A1 y A2, año), (A1 et al., año)
- Lista de referencias: TODOS los autores completos
- NUNCA "et al." en la lista final
- URL completa con https:// o DOI como https://doi.org/xxxxx
- NUNCA inventar autores, años, volumenes, paginas ni URLs

### Seccion 6 - Fidelidad de fuentes (lineas 128-158)

Ampliado el 2026-10-12. PROHIBIDO:
- Cambiar autores, apellidos, iniciales
- Cambiar titulo, revista, volumen, paginas, año
- Cambiar URL o DOI
- "Mejorar" o combinar referencias
- Completar con datos no verificados
- Reescribir "para que suene mejor"

Incluye ejemplo BIEN y ejemplo MAL (con caso Groth).

### Seccion 7 - Delegacion a subagentes (lineas 159-190)

Version neutral (actualizada 2026-10-12):
- Opcion 1: delegate_task (interno, rapido, hereda SOUL)
- Opcion 2: hermes_herald (cross-profile, con bug de relay)
- Libre eleccion segun tarea
- Si herald falla: reintentar con delegate_task

---

## 5. MECANISMOS DE DELEGACION

Orchestrator tiene 2 mecanismos disponibles (configurable libremente):

### Mecanismo 1 - delegate_task (interno)

- Crea subagentes en el mismo proceso del padre.
- Heredan el SOUL del padre (incluidas reglas APA y fidelidad).
- Rapido, puede paralelizar en batch.
- Sin bugs conocidos.
- Uso: delegate_task(goal="<tarea>")

### Mecanismo 2 - hermes_herald (cross-profile)

- Invoca los perfiles research/writer/developer REALES.
- Cada uno con su SOUL propio y su memoria.
- Mas lento, secuencial.
- BUG CONOCIDO: el relay de respuestas puede devolver vacio.
- Uso: dispatch_chat(profile="research", message="<tarea>")

### Eleccion

- Tareas rapidas: delegate_task.
- Tareas que necesiten reglas especificas del target: hermes_herald.
- Si herald falla: reintentar con delegate_task.

---

## 6. ENRUTAMIENTO POR TEMAS (profile_routes)

Cada tema de Telegram enruta al perfil correcto:

Escribes en Tema General    -> Orchestrator responde
Escribes en Tema research   -> Research responde
Escribes en Tema writer     -> Writer responde
Escribes en Tema developer  -> Developer responde

Implementado en /home/droidmaster/.hermes/config.yaml (nivel RAIZ).
Campo bot_profile: orchestrator es OBLIGATORIO para que matchee.
Sin el, las rutas no se activan porque el bot del grupo es @HermesPro.

---

## 7. BUGS Y LIMITACIONES CONOCIDAS

### Bug 1 - Herald relay vacio (ACTIVO)

Sintoma: dispatch_chat devuelve respuestas vacias.
Evidencia: 22 runs en ledger, TODOS con output_preview="".
Causa: desconocida, posible version v1.2.0 con bug.
Workaround: usar delegate_task.
Pendiente: actualizar/reinstalar el plugin o reportar al autor.

### Bug 2 - Fallback qwen3.8-27b (MITIGADO)

Sintoma: cuando Gemini falla, el fallback devuelve 413 (contexto grande).
Causa: qwen3.8-27b tiene contexto pequeno.
Mitigacion parcial: fallback.min_switch_reset_seconds=120 en config.
Pendiente: cambiar a openai/gpt-oss-120b (128k contexto).

### Bug 3 - skills.auto_load no regenera snapshot

Sintoma: en Hermes 0.21.5 + Termux/proot, el snapshot de skills no se
regenera al reiniciar el gateway.
Solucion adoptada: poner reglas en SOUL.md en vez de skills.

### Limitacion 1 - RAM compartida

Un solo Gateway sirve 5 perfiles. Si cae, caen todos (bot viejo + nuevo).
RAM actual: ~630 MB disponibles de 3653 MB.

### Limitacion 2 - Hermes 0.21.5 sin agent_profiles

No soporta delegate_task(profile="X"). Solo delegate_task(goal="X").
Por eso Herald fue necesario para cross-profile.

---

## 8. PENDIENTES

### Prioridad ALTA (seguridad)

- [ ] Rotar GOOGLE_API_KEY (expuesta en logs)
- [ ] Rotar HONCHO_API_KEY (expuesta en honcho.json texto plano)
- [ ] Rotar AIRTABLE_API_KEY (expuesta en logs)
- [ ] Limpiar .zsh_history (1.19 MB con posible contenido sensible)

### Prioridad MEDIA (mejoras)

- [ ] Arreglar Herald (actualizar plugin o reportar bug al autor)
- [ ] Cambiar fallback qwen3.8-27b por openai/gpt-oss-120b
- [ ] Desactivar kanban.dispatch_in_gateway (no lo usamos)
- [ ] Diagnosticar caidas del Gateway (logcat sin analizar)

### Prioridad BAJA (mantenimiento)

- [ ] Re-indexar vault Obsidian (mensual)
- [ ] Revisar backups de perfiles (rotacion)
- [ ] Verificar integridad state.db de cada perfil

---

## 9. COMO RETOMAR EN OTRA SESION

1. Verificar que el Gateway este corriendo:
   cat ~/.hermes/gateway_state.json | grep served_profiles
   Debe mostrar: default, developer, orchestrator, research, writer

2. Verificar tamanos de SOUL.md:
   wc -c ~/.hermes/profiles/*/SOUL.md
   Esperado:
     orchestrator: ~8433
     research:     ~5643
     writer:       ~4502
     developer:    ~1632

3. Verificar profile_routes en config RAIZ:
   grep -c profile_routes ~/.hermes/config.yaml
   Debe dar >= 1

4. Si el Gateway esta caido:
   cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent
   setsid ./venv/bin/hermes gateway run > ~/.hermes/logs/gateway-manual.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &

5. Probar cada agente en su tema de Telegram:
   - Tema General:     "hola"
   - Tema research:    "quien eres"
   - Tema writer:      "quien eres"
   - Tema developer:   "quien eres"

6. Revisar pendientes de arriba (seccion 8).

---

## 10. APRENDIZAJES CLAVE

1. profile_routes va en el config RAIZ, no en el del perfil.
2. El campo bot_profile es OBLIGATORIO cuando el bot no es el default.
3. Honcho comparte memoria por peerName - cada perfil necesita el suyo.

content:
# Resumen

El artículo analiza el desarrollo del emicizumab, un anticuerpo biespecífico que imita la función del factor VIII para tratar la hemofilia A, un logro reconocido con el Premio Lasker-DeBakey de Investigación Médica Clínica 2026.

# Puntos clave

1. Los tratamientos tradicionales para la hemofilia A dependían del reemplazo del factor VIII, el cual presenta limitaciones como una vida media corta y el desarrollo de anticuerpos neutralizantes (inhibidores) en hasta un tercio de los pacientes.
2. Kunihiro Hattori, Tomoyuki Igawa y Takehisa Kitazawa desarrollaron un anticuerpo biespecífico que une simultáneamente el factor IXa y el factor X para imitar la actividad cofactor del factor VIIIa.
3. Tras evaluar aproximadamente 40,000 anticuerpos biespecíficos y optimizar sus propiedades, el equipo superó los desafíos de fabricación mediante mutaciones electrostáticas para evitar el emparejamiento aleatorio de cadenas pesadas y ligeras.
4. El emicizumab (ACE910) permite la profilaxis subcutánea con administraciones poco frecuentes y resulta eficaz tanto en pacientes con inhibidores como sin ellos.
5. Los ensayos clínicos pivotal HAVEN confirmaron una reducción drástica de las hemorragias, aunque también identificaron señales de seguridad relacionadas con eventos trombóticos al combinarse con dosis altas de concentrados del complejo de protrombina activada.

# Datos clave

- Premio Lasker-DeBakey de Investigación Médica Clínica 2026.
- Se examinaron aproximadamente 40,000 anticuerpos biespecíficos en la fase de descubrimiento.
- El anticuerpo biespecífico emicizumab fue aprobado en Estados Unidos en 2017 y posteriormente en Europa, Japón y otros países.

# Conexiones

Relacionado con mi conocimiento existente:

- [[Coagulación]]
- [[2026-09-30-随手记录-1d154a1d]]
- [[structured-content]]
- [[infographic]]
- [[Venta]]

# Acciones

- Evitar el uso prolongado de altas dosis de concentrado del complejo de protrombina activada en pacientes que reciben profilaxis con emicizumab para prevenir eventos trombóticos.
- Utilizar emicizumab como profilaxis de rutina subcutánea con administración semanal, quincenal o mensual para mejorar la calidad de vida en pacientes con hemofilia A.

Reengineering Coagulation with a Bispecific Antibody
Flora Peyvandi, M.D., Ph.D.1,2
For decades, the treatment of hemophilia A rested
on a single principle: replacing factor VIII (see Key
Concepts), the missing clotting factor. Plasma-
derived and recombinant factor VIII concentrates
transformed a once-fatal disease into a manage-
able chronic condition through prophylaxis and
treatment. But factor VIII has a relatively short
half-life and thus is administered through fre -
quent intravenous infusions, and neutralizing
anti–factor VIII antibodies (inhibitors) that render
replacement therapy ineffective develop in up to
one third of patients with severe hemophilia A.1-3
By showing that the coagulation cascade could be
activated in the absence of factor VIII, Kunihiro
Hattori, Tomoyuki Igawa, and Takehisa Kitazawa
(of Chugai Pharmaceutical) overcame these limi-
tations. They developed a bispecific antibody that
mimics blood coagulation factor VIII, an achieve-
ment recognized by the 2026 Lasker–DeBakey
Clinical Medical Research Award.
In 2000, it had been established that activated
factor VIII (factor VIIIa) binds both activated fac-
tor IX (factor IXa) and factor X and thereby ac -
celerates prothrombinase complex formation and
thrombin generation, presumably by modulating
the catalytic activity of factor IXa and bringing
factor IXa and factor X into close proximity.4 Hat-
tori, who was working on therapeutic antibodies
at Chugai, reasoned that an antibody that simul-
taneously binds factor IXa and factor X and posi-
tions them appropriately might reproduce the co-
factor activity of factor VIIIa despite factor VIIIa
having an entirely different molecular structure.
His idea was also built on the earlier observation
that a cofactor, protein S, can regulate the action
of an enzyme toward its substrate by controlling
their spatial positioning.5
The concept was bold. Conventional antibod-
ies recognize a single target through two identi-
cal antigen-binding arms. Hattori envisaged a
molecule that could bind two different coagula-
tion factors simultaneously while reproducing
the highly dynamic spatial organization of the
intrinsic tenase complex (made up of factor VIIIa
and factor IXa and assembled on the plasma
membrane of platelets; see the full definition in
Key Concepts). Moreover, factor VIIIa accelerates
coagulation through multiple molecular interac-
tions, many of which were poorly understood at
the time. Reproducing this function with an anti-
body that recognizes only a single epitope on
each target seemed improbable.6
The team adopted an empirical strategy. They
initially generated and screened hundreds of
anti–factor IXa and anti–factor X bispecific anti-
bodies and then expanded the effort to generate
and screen thousands of bispecific antibodies.
They ultimately generated and screened approxi-
mately 40,000 bispecific antibodies (Fig. 1A).6,8
Early candidates substantially shortened the ac-
tivated partial-thromboplastin time (aPTT), but
an important realization soon changed the di -
rection of the project. Unlike factor VIII re -
placement, improvement in aPTT did not reli -
ably predict in vivo hemostatic efficacy. 4 The
investigators, led by Kitazawa, therefore shifted
their focus from conventional coagulation as -
says to direct measurements of factor Xa genera-
tion and in vivo bleeding control.
Igawa played a central role in the iterative
molecular engineering that followed. Thousands
of different antibodies were systematically re -
fined to improve not only factor VIII–mimetic
activity (factor Xa generation) but also pharmaco-
kinetic properties, stability, solubility, and pre -
dicted immunogenicity. Weak binding affinity
proved desirable because effective catalysis re -
quires transient interactions that permit coagu -
lation complexes to assemble and dissociate
normally. Each engineering cycle introduced
combinations of amino acid substitutions de -
signed to improve one property without compro-
mising another, which resulted in a molecule
with sufficient factor VIII–mimetic activity for
clinical development (Fig. 1A).4,8

Factor VIII
A large glycoprotein synthesized in liver sinusoidal and vascular endothe-
lial cells that participates in the coagulation cascade. The active form of
factor VIII (factor VIIIa), generated by the action of thrombin (activated
factor II), is a cofactor for the serine protease factor IXa within the intrinsic
tenase complex. The intrinsic tenase complex is essential for the genera-
tion of thrombin, the final enzyme of the coagulation cascade necessary
for clot formation (so thrombin is activated by factor VIIIa; in an amplifica-
tion reaction, it also activates factor VIII). In the circulation, the large ma-
jority of factor VIII molecules are bound to von Willebrand factor, which is
necessary for its stability. Membrane-dependent assembly of the intrinsic
tenase complex requires release of factor VIII from von Willebrand factor.
Abnormalities of the factor VIII gene (located on the X chromosome)
cause hemophilia A, a bleeding disorder. Conversely, factor VIII levels can
double, triple, or quadruple during acute-phase responses and pregnancy,
increasing the risk of thrombosis.
Bispecific antibody
An antibody with two binding sites directed at two different antigens or
two different epitopes on the same antigen. Its effects are determined
by its targets and structure. Bispecific antibodies may be full-length IgG
or antibody fragments. Full-length bispecific antibodies are made with
the use of strategies that ensure correct pairing of two different heavy
and two different light chains, each with its own variable binding do-
main. Bispecific antibodies in clinical use include blinatumomab
(for acute lymphoblastic leukemia), emicizumab (for hemophilia A),
and faricimab (for neovascular age-related macular degeneration).
Thrombin
An enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin to create a blood clot. It is gen-
erated from circulating prothrombin (factor II) by the action of factor Xa
(activated factor X). A burst of thrombin generation is a critical step for sta-
ble clot formation. The activation of factors VIII and IX drives a robust burst
of thrombin; genetic deficiency of factor VIII or factor IX causes hemophilia.
Intrinsic tenase complex
An enzymatic complex of the coagulation cascade composed of activated
factor VIII (factor VIIIa) and activated factor IX (factor IXa). The intrinsic
tenase complex assembles on the phosphatidylserine-exposing mem-
brane of activated platelets in the presence of Ca2+. Once assembled, the
complex activates factor X: through a docking process scaffolded by factor
VIII, factor IXa and factor X are brought together and positioned in a way
that permits factor IXa to activate factor X. Thus, factor VIIIa accelerates
factor X activation and thrombin generation. In hemophilia A, factor VIII
is absent or dysfunctional, which impairs hemostasis.

After its engineering and improvement, emicizumab
(originally called ACE910) was developed for subcuta -
neous prophylaxis with dose administration every

tion of emicizumab, which simultaneously binds acti -
vated factor IX (factor IXa) and factor X, functionally
replacing the cofactor activity of factor VIIIa. By bridg -
ing factor IXa and factor X, emicizumab promotes acti-
vation of factor X, which results in thrombin genera -
tion and restoration of effective hemostasis.

    presupuesto_income_ejecutado AS "IT (CUP) |",

content:
# ¿Qué es el Capitalismo?

El capitalismo es un sistema económico, social y político en el que los medios de producción son de propiedad privada y se busca obtener beneficio principalmente a través del mercado y la competencia.

## Características Principales
- **Propiedad Privada:** Los individuos o empresas poseen los medios de producción (tierras, fábricas, herramientas).
- **Libertad Económica:** Libertad de producir, vender, comprar e invertir buscando el beneficio propio.
- **Economía de Mercado:** Precios determinados por la oferta y la demanda, sin planificación central.
- **Competencia:** Empresas compitiendo por ofrecer mejores productos y servicios.
- **Búsqueda de Beneficio:** Obtención de ganancias como motor de inversión, crecimiento e innovación.

## Funcionamiento
1. Idea o recurso → 2. Inversión de capital → 3. Venta en mercado → 4. Obtención de ganancia → 5. Reinversión.

## Ventajas vs. Desafíos
- **Ventajas:** Innovación, variedad de productos, incentivo al esfuerzo individual, empleo y crecimiento.
- **Desafíos:** Desigualdad en la distribución de la riqueza, prioridad del beneficio sobre el bienestar social/ambiental, riesgos de monopolios, acceso desigual a oportunidades.

## Idea Central
Equilibrio entre **Crecimiento Económico** y **Bienestar Social**.

> "En el capitalismo, el motor que mueve al mundo es el interés propio." — Adam Smith

# Errores en Finanzas Personales

Infografía que resume los errores más frecuentes que afectan la salud financiera personal.

## Errores identificados:
- **Gastar más de lo que ganas:** Desequilibrio presupuestario fundamental.
- **No ahorrar y no invertir:** Falta de fondo de emergencia y crecimiento patrimonial.
- **Mal uso de las tarjetas de crédito:** Deuda de alto interés por consumo innecesario.
- **Gastar en vicios:** Drenaje constante de recursos.
- **Solo tener una fuente de ingresos:** Alta vulnerabilidad ante imprevistos.
- **No llevar registro de gastos:** Desconocimiento de los hábitos de consumo.
- **Mantenerte en tu zona de confort:** Falta de evolución o búsqueda de nuevas oportunidades.

content:
# Resumen

Infografía médica que explica detalladamente la prueba de Coombs directa e indirecta, abarcando su detección, función, indicaciones clínicas, interpretación de resultados y procedimiento.

# Puntos clave

1. La prueba de Coombs directa detecta anticuerpos o complemento adheridos a la superficie de los eritrocitos in vivo.
2. La prueba de Coombs indirecta detecta anticuerpos libres en el suero contra antígenos eritrocitarios in vitro.
3. La prueba directa se indica en anemia hemolítica autoinmune, reacciones transfusionales y enfermedad hemolítica del recién nacido.
4. La prueba indirecta se utiliza para tamizaje pretransfusional y control prenatal.
5. La interpretación positiva de la prueba directa indica hemólisis inmune, mientras que la indirecta previene reacciones transfusionales y vigila embarazos en riesgo.

# Datos clave

- Coombs directo detecta anticuerpos adheridos a los eritrocitos in vivo
- Coombs indirecto detecta anticuerpos libres en el suero
- El procedimiento consta de 5 pasos: muestra, incubación, observación, interpretación y correlación clínica

# Resumen

El aprendizaje automático es una rama de la inteligencia artificial enfocada en el desarrollo de algoritmos estadísticos capaces de aprender de los datos para realizar tareas sin programación explícita.

# Puntos clave

1. El aprendizaje automático permite a los sistemas generalizar a partir de datos no vistos y realizar tareas sin programación explícita.
2. Se fundamenta en la estadística y los métodos de optimización matemática.
3. El aprendizaje supervisado utiliza datos de ejemplo con salidas deseadas proporcionadas por un maestro.
4. El aprendizaje no supervisado busca patrones ocultos en datos sin etiquetas.
5. El aprendizaje por refuerzo implica la interacción con un entorno dinámico para maximizar recompensas.
6. El término fue acuñado en 1959 por Arthur Samuel, pionero de IBM.

# Datos clave

- El término machine learning fue acuñado en 1959.
- Arthur Samuel fue el pionero de IBM que acuñó el término y creó un programa para el juego de damas.
- El campo floreció como disciplina propia en los años 90.

# Contenido original

# Machine Learning (Aprendizaje Automático)

URL: https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning

El aprendizaje automático (o *machine learning*) es un campo de estudio dentro de la inteligencia artificial que se ocupa del desarrollo y estudio de algoritmos estadísticos que pueden aprender de los datos y generalizar a datos no vistos, permitiendo realizar tareas sin ser programados explícitamente.

## Fundamentos
La estadística y los métodos de optimización matemática constituyen los fundamentos del aprendizaje automático. La minería de datos es un campo relacionado, centrado en el análisis exploratorio de datos mediante aprendizaje no supervisado.

## Paradigmas de Aprendizaje
Los enfoques de aprendizaje automático se dividen tradicionalmente en tres categorías:

1. **Aprendizaje Supervisado**: La computadora recibe datos de ejemplo junto con las salidas deseadas (etiquetas) proporcionadas por un "maestro". El objetivo es aprender una regla general que mapee entradas a salidas.
2. **Aprendizaje No Supervisado**: No se proporcionan etiquetas al algoritmo, dejándolo por su cuenta para encontrar estructuras o patrones ocultos en los datos.
3. **Aprendizaje por Refuerzo**: Un programa interactúa con un entorno dinámico para realizar una tarea específica. Recibe recompensas como retroalimentación que intenta maximizar, aprendiendo así a través de la experiencia.

## Historia
El término "machine learning" fue acuñado en 1959 por Arthur Samuel, pionero de IBM en juegos de computadora e IA, quien introdujo uno de los primeros programas capaces de calcular probabilidades de ganar en el juego de damas. Aunque sus raíces se encuentran en estudios anteriores de procesos cognitivos humanos, el campo floreció como disciplina propia en los años 90, desplazando su enfoque desde métodos simbólicos hacia enfoques estadísticos y probabilísticos.

content:
# Resumen

La inteligencia artificial es una disciplina informática que busca crear sistemas capaces de imitar la inteligencia humana para realizar tareas complejas, aprender de la experiencia y automatizar procesos intelectuales.

# Puntos clave

1. Es una disciplina de las ciencias de la computación orientada a crear máquinas que imiten la inteligencia humana.
2. Permite a los sistemas aprender de la experiencia, adaptarse a nuevas entradas y realizar tareas como reconocimiento de voz y toma de decisiones.
3. Abarca múltiples subcampos que van desde el aprendizaje general hasta áreas específicas como el diagnóstico médico y la creación artística.
4. Utiliza tecnologías en constante evolución como el aprendizaje profundo, redes neuronales y procesamiento del lenguaje natural.
5. Emplea diversos modelos de aprendizaje como el automático, por refuerzo, profundo y supervisado.
6. Ha propiciado el surgimiento de nuevos campos de estudio como la roboética y la ética de las máquinas para un manejo responsable.

# Datos clave

- La inteligencia artificial se abrevia como IA o AI en inglés.
- Incluye subcampos como el reconocimiento de voz, ajedrez, demostración de teoremas y diagnóstico de enfermedades.
- Se apoya en tecnologías como redes neuronales y aprendizaje profundo.

- Analizar el impacto ético y el manejo responsable de las tecnologías de IA.
- Explorar las aplicaciones prácticas de la inteligencia artificial en la vida cotidiana.

# Contenido original

# Inteligencia artificial

URL: https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inteligencia_artificial

La inteligencia artificial, abreviada como IA o AI (por su nombre en inglés: artificial intelligence), en el contexto de las ciencias de la computación, es una disciplina y un conjunto de capacidades cognoscitivas e intelectuales expresadas por sistemas informáticos o combinaciones de algoritmos cuyo propósito es la creación de máquinas que imiten la inteligencia humana.

Estas tecnologías permiten que las máquinas aprendan de la experiencia, se adapten a nuevas entradas y realicen tareas humanas como el reconocimiento de voz, la toma de decisiones, la traducción de idiomas o la visión por computadora.

En la actualidad, la inteligencia artificial abarca una gran variedad de subcampos. Estos van desde áreas de propósito general, aprendizaje y percepción, a otras más específicas como el reconocimiento de voz, el juego de ajedrez, la demostración de teoremas matemáticos, el cálculo y la resolución de problemas aritméticos y algebraicos, la escritura de poesía, la composición musical, la creación artística, las reglas gramaticales y lingüísticas o el diagnóstico de enfermedades. La inteligencia artificial sintetiza y automatiza tareas que en principio son intelectuales y, por lo tanto, es potencialmente relevante para cualquier ámbito de actividades intelectuales humanas. En este sentido, es un campo genuinamente universal, además, la IA se encuentra en constante evolución gracias al desarrollo de tecnologías como el aprendizaje profundo, redes neuronales y procesamiento del lenguaje natural, lo cual permite un avance acelerado en su capacidad para resolver problemas complejos.

La arquitectura de las inteligencias artificiales y los procesos por los cuales aprenden, se mejoran y se implementan en algún área de interés varían según el enfoque de utilidad que se les quiera dar, pero de manera general, estos van desde la ejecución de sencillos algoritmos hasta la interconexión de complejas redes neuronales artificiales que intentan replicar los circuitos neuronales del cerebro humano y que aprenden mediante diferentes modelos de aprendizaje tales como el aprendizaje automático, el aprendizaje por refuerzo, el aprendizaje profundo y el aprendizaje supervisado.

Por otro lado, el desarrollo y aplicación de la inteligencia artificial en muchos aspectos de la vida cotidiana también ha propiciado la creación de nuevos campos de estudio como la roboética y la ética de las máquinas, que abordan aspectos relacionados con la ética en la inteligencia artificial y que se encargan de analizar cómo los avances en este tipo de tecnologías impactarían en diversos ámbitos de la vida, así como el manejo responsable y ético que se les debería dar a los mismos.

# Sábado

> [!abstract] Definición
> El sistema solar está compuesto por ocho planetas principales que orbitan alrededor del Sol.

## Desarrollo & Detalles

Los ocho planetas, ordenados por su distancia creciente al Sol, son:

1. **Mercurio**: El más cercano al Sol y el más pequeño.
2. **Venus**: El segundo en distancia, conocido como el planeta gemelo de la Tierra.
3. **Tierra**: Nuestro hogar, el único lugar conocido con vida.
4. **Marte**: Conocido como el planeta rojo.
5. **Júpiter**: El planeta más grande del sistema solar.
6. **Saturno**: Famoso por su espectacular sistema de anillos.
7. **Urano**: Un gigante helado con un eje de rotación inusual.
8. **Neptuno**: El planeta más lejano, un gigante de hielo regido por vientos supersónicos.

## Aplicación Práctica
Esta lista representa la estructura fundamental de nuestro vecindario cósmico según la definición actual de la Unión Astronómica Internacional.

## Conexiones & Notas Relacionadas

title: TEMPLATE
snippet: # Task Note Template Use this template when creating or repairing a task folder. Every task folder must have all three files. ## RESUME.md ```markdown...
content:
# Task Note Template

Use this template when creating or repairing a task folder. Every task folder must have all three files.

## RESUME.md

```markdown
# <Task Name> Resume

Last heartbeat: <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM TZ>
Task: <one-line description of the task>
Current status: <active | stalled | complete>
Next action: <one concrete next step>
Key files:
- Tasks/<task-name>/RESUME.md
- Tasks/<task-name>/CHECKLIST.md
- Tasks/<task-name>/DOCS.md

Restart note: <what a fresh session needs to know to pick this up>
```

## CHECKLIST.md

```markdown
# <Task Name> Checklist

- [ ] Step 1: <describe the step>
- [ ] Step 2: <describe the step>
- [ ] Verification: confirm the work is correct
```

## DOCS.md

```markdown
# <Task Name> Docs

## Goal
<what this task is trying to achieve>

## Important decisions
<key choices made and why>

## Files that matter
<paths to the important files>

## Gotchas and failure modes
<things that can go wrong>

## Notes for the next session
<anything a fresh session should know>
```

## Rules

- Keep notes short and scannable.
- Always update `Last heartbeat` when touching an active task.
- Never leave a folder with only one or two of the three core notes.
- The validator will auto-create missing notes from this template.

---

# 📊 Informe Financiero — Septiembre 2026

### 💰 1. Resumen de Ingresos y Gastos
*   **Total de Ingresos:** `68,300 CUP` *(Registrado en `Presupuesto_septiembre.md`)*
*   **Total de Gastos:** `25,265 CUP`
*   **Saldo Neto (Ahorro del Mes):** `+43,035 CUP` 

---

### 📂 2. Desglose de Gastos por Categoría
A continuación se detallan los montos reales ejecutados por categoría durante el mes actual:

*   🥩 **Alimentación:** `8,000 CUP` *(Categoría con mayor gasto)*
*   👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 **Familia:** `3,000 CUP`
*   🚌 **Transporte:** `2,000 CUP`
*   🎉 **Ocio:** `2,000 CUP`
*   🏠 **Hogar:** `2,000 CUP`
*   🧼 **Aseo:** `1,500 CUP`
*   👤 **Personal:** `1,500 CUP`
*   📱 **Teléfono:** `1,500 CUP`
*   🏥 **Salud:** `1,000 CUP`
*   🤝 **Préstamo:** `1,000 CUP`
*   📦 **Otros:** `1,000 CUP`
*   💡 **Electricidad:** `500 CUP`

> **💡 Categoría con mayor gasto:** **Alimentación** encabeza la lista con un total de `8,000 CUP`, representando una parte importante de tu presupuesto mensual.

---

### 📈 3. Comparativa con el Mes Anterior (Agosto 2026)
*   **Ingresos:** En agosto tus ingresos ejecutados fueron de `25,700 CUP`. En septiembre experimentaste un crecimiento notable alcanzando los `68,300 CUP`, lo que representa un incremento sustancial en tu flujo de caja.
*   **Gastos:** En agosto el gasto total ejecutado fue de `25,700 CUP`. En septiembre los gastos se mantuvieron estables en `25,265 CUP`, logrando una excelente contención del gasto a pesar del aumento significativo de los ingresos.
*   **Capacidad de Ahorro:** Pasaste de un saldo neto deficitario o ajustado en agosto (`-2,980 CUP`) a un **saldo neto altamente positivo de `+43,035 CUP`** en septiembre.

---

### 🎯 4. Consejos Prácticos para Ahorrar (Basados en tu Mayor Gasto)
Dado que **Alimentación** (`8,000 CUP`) es tu principal categoría de gasto, te sugiero las siguientes acciones prácticas:

1.  **Compra planificada y al por mayor:** Intenta realizar compras centralizadas en ferias o mercados mayoristas al inicio de mes, aprovechando los precios más bajos en granos, cárnicos y productos secos para evitar compras de última hora a precios minoristas elevados.
2.  **Optimiza el consumo semanal:** Diseña un menú semanal básico para reducir el desperdicio de alimentos y controlar mejor la adquisición de productos perecederos.
3.  **Monitoreo diario de gastos hormiga:** Aunque la alimentación principal está controlada, asegúrate de registrar y auditar pequeños consumos en la calle o ferias intermedias que puedan sumar montos innecesarios al final de la semana.

* **Saldo Neto:** +11,175 CUP *(Superávit)*

### 🛍️ 2. Desglose de Gastos por Categoría (Septiembre)
Durante este inicio de mes se han registrado las siguientes transacciones:

* **[[Alimentación]]:** 1,200 CUP *(Frijoles colorados)*

> 🏆 **Categoría con mayor gasto:** **Alimentación** (con un total de **1,200 CUP**, representando el **59.26%** de los gastos totales del mes).

---

### 📥 3. Desglose de Ingresos por Fuente (Septiembre)
* **[[Salario]] (Vacaciones):** 13,200 CUP *(Ingresado a través de BPA7734)*

---

### 📈 4. Comparativa con el Mes Anterior (Agosto 2026)
* *Nota:* Los datos de agosto muestran un volumen de transacciones significativamente mayor al cierre del mes (con gastos importantes en Ocio/Playa por 7,580 CUP, Cooperativa por 8,000 CUP, y Alimentación/Comida varias por 5,000 CUP, además de un ingreso por Salario de 25,700 CUP). 
* Al comparar el ritmo actual con los primeros días de agosto, el flujo de gastos en septiembre arranca de manera **mucho más moderada**, permitiendo conservar un saldo neto positivo considerable gracias al ingreso por vacaciones de 13,200 CUP.

---

### 💡 5. Consejos Prácticos para Ahorrar
Basado en tus categorías de mayor gasto actual (principalmente *Alimentación*):

1. **Planificación de Compras al por Mayor:** Dado que los productos alimenticios concentran la mayor parte de tus egresos (como los frijoles y provisiones), intenta programar compras centralizadas en mercados mayoristas al inicio del ciclo de ingresos para conseguir mejores precios por volumen.
2. **Optimización de Servicios y Suscripciones:** Aunque el gasto en telefonía (325 CUP) es bajo en comparación, aprovecha siempre bonos de recarga internacional o promociones vigentes para estirar el saldo móvil el mayor tiempo posible.
3. **Fondo de Reserva para Imprevistos:** Con el saldo neto positivo actual (+11,175 CUP), te sugiero destinar un porcentaje fijo (por ejemplo, el 50%) directamente a una cuenta de ahorro o fondo de emergencia antes de que comiencen a acumularse nuevos gastos cotidianos.
